A relic of the Savoy cyclone, in the shape of a deed from J. J. Duderstadt to S. J. Thomas, was found a few days ago in a cedar brake in the Indian Territory, north of Paris, and forwarded to our County Clerk by Judge Eaton. The deed was so much defaced as to be unreadable, every letter of the inscription being illegible. It was found on lot No. 9 in block 475 of the town of Savoy, dated April, 1888.

Mrs. W. B. (Bennetta Connally) Duncan stated, in an interview with the author more than half a century since she stood at her mother's side and listened to the story of the tornado as it bore down upon the little town of Savoy, 1888, carrying death and destruction in its path. It was the most distressing calamity ever witnessed in this section. Lives were lost, property destroyed, and bodies bruised and mangled in every conceivable manner. The storm struck the town at 10 o'clock and lasted all night. The storm struck the town at 10 o'clock and lasted all night. The foundations of the houses were swept away. About twelve houses, besides many outhouses, were demolished. The storm, it seemed, needing to come down from the clouds, in a frenzied and concentrated rush of lightning, thunder and hail at the same time. The trees were uprooted and electricity seemed to be flying through and through the dark and heavy atmosphere. The intensity of the darkness and the density of the atmosphere was almost indescribable. The passenger train on the T. and P. railroad passed through in the midst of the tornado, and was the means of carrying the news to the outside world. At one time it was thought that over two thousand persons were on the ground. Physicians from Sherman and Denison came at once with money and medicine.
